*edit

Scope / purpose of this bag. Hopefully this bag will keep me rested, fed, and warm for three days with little or no help from anyone. Light enough to carry if needed although I certainly would prefer to use my car or bike.

Water

Two day supply of water (4.5 liters) and a water filter. Coffee filters to strain muddy water if needed so the Sawyer filter doesn't get gunked up.

Food

3 day supply of food. MSR whisperlite Universal stove and 600 milliliters white gas. Stove will also run on kerosene, butane, propane, and gasoline if needed . GSI solo pot kit for boiling water, it also includes a bowl and spork

Clothing

Base layer top and bottom of polypropylene long johns, wool socks, wool underwear and wool t-shirt. I also have an extra pair of pants, nylon Columbia convertible.

Sleep system

Suisse-sport -1 degree sleeping bag, Sol Escape bivvy and Therm-a-Rest Z rest sleeping pad. The sleeping bag is not rated for the winter temperatures here, so until I invest in a better one I can use the Sol bivvy inside the bag for an extra layer of warmth. I also keep a wool blanket in my car.

Shelter

Ferrino Pumori 2 person tent. Heavier than I'd like, but it is an amazing winter tent.

First Aid

Various over-the-counter products including sunscreen, bandages, tape, scissors, and tweezers. I've also included a SAM splint in case someone or myself suffered a fracture.

Hygiene

Hand sanitizer, floss, toothpaste, toothbrush, body wash, deodorant, TP, razor, and shaving cream.

Misc

Lighter, headlamp, swing liteflex umbrella (bag has built in rain cover too), 50 feet cord, and plenty of cash with small bills.

Firearms

It's worth noting that while I did not include firearms in the kit I have pistols and long guns available. My thinking is most evacuations are not due to civil unrest nor do they lead to it (although we have seen otherwise, think Katrina hurricane and LA riots for example). If I did believe there was a possibility of unrest I would bring firearms.

Knife

I have a nice Spyderco as part of my EDC.

I don't have a need for a sleeping pad in my bug out bag.

The idea is to help you rest and be more alert the next day. Something raised off the ground can go miles to that. Yes- more food or medical or water filters would be options, as would a local map or batteries, but don't completely discount having a pad as it is extremely lightweight and being waterproof- can be makeshift shelter material.

I own pads, both a zlite and an expensive inflatable. I do mountaineering and backcountry elk hunting. For my BOB, I need to be fast and light. I'm not going for comfort, I'm going for packability. I carry a poncho, and an upgraded space blanket. It's thicker and is OD green on the other side further increasing my camouflage. The most sleeping I would be doing if I needed this bag, would be for short 2-4 hour naps between fast walking.

That's the thing. This isn't set up as if I'm running for my life, most emergencies don't require that. If that happens I can shed gear. But I'd rather pack it initially.

I also have an expensive inflatable which takes up less space, but with this bulkier one I don't have to worry about punctures.

I use a 50 liter pack for 2-3 night stays in the hills where comfort is in mind. I've overnighted with technical rock gear, a 60 meter rope, and my bivy gear all packed into a 50 liter. That pack is huge. I use an army surplus assault pack for my BOB. I have caffeine and high energy foods to get me home or to my caches for resupply. What my BOB doesn't have, is the ability for me to live out of. I only have 15,000 kcal and 2 litters of water, but I have tabs to purify more. I have cash money in the pack too. In most crisis situations, I would likely have time to pack a larger bag with more comfort items; sleeping pad and stove. But with a BOB, it's grab and go. No time for anything but the rifle, chest rig, and this pack.

Also, why you got an umbrella? An army surplus poncho is both a tent/ground cloth and it's also weather proofing. Take a look at the SOL double bivy or Titan emergency bivy. Mylar is also camouflage for infrared cameras.

Why are bug out bags specifically designed for 72 hours? It appears to be the standard in survival prepping. Just wondering, thanks.

A 72-hour bag is purposed exactly the way it was named: it should be crafted to get you through a 72-hour survival scenario. The reason why many survivalists pick the 3-day window is because in most cases, you will be rescued and back in civilization by the third day. Also, packing for 72 hours is rather easy, as there are a few categories of provisions that you can survive without over the course of 3 days. Any amount of time beyond that, and you’re going to need to pack differently.
